title: How Much Caffeine Is in Green Tea? (vs Coffee, Matcha & Black Tea)
h1: How much caffeine is in green tea?
meta_description: An 8 oz cup of steeped green tea has about 25–45 mg of caffeine (typically ~35 mg) — less than black tea, matcha, or coffee. Full comparison inside.
keywords: how much caffeine in green tea
green tea caffeine vs black tea
body_html:
An 8 oz cup of steeped green tea contains about 25–45 mg of caffeine — typically around 35 mg. That's roughly a third of a cup of coffee (~95 mg) and about two-thirds of a cup of black tea (~50 mg).

What changes how much caffeine ends up in your cup

Green tea's caffeine isn't one fixed number — it's a range, because brewing choices and the leaf itself both move it. The main variables:

  • Steep time. Caffeine is one of the fastest compounds to extract from tea leaves, so a longer steep pulls out more of it. A quick 1-minute steep sits toward the low end of the range; a full 3-minute steep pushes toward the high end.
  • Water temperature. Hotter water extracts caffeine faster. Green tea is typically brewed at 165–185°F (74–85°C) — cooler than black tea's near-boiling water — which is one reason green tea's typical caffeine lands lower than black tea's, even before steep time is factored in.
  • Leaf grade and cultivar. Younger leaves and buds, used in higher grades of sencha and gyokuro, tend to carry more caffeine than older, coarser leaves picked later in the season.
  • Loose leaf vs. tea bag. More surface area extracts faster, so finely cut bagged tea can release caffeine a little quicker than whole-leaf tea over the same steep time.
  • Amount of leaf used. A heaping teaspoon per 8 oz extracts more caffeine than a level one, the same way a stronger pour-over has more caffeine than a weak one.

None of these variables push green tea outside its overall 25–45 mg range for a standard 8 oz cup — they explain why the number moves within that range rather than why one source says 20 mg and another says 60 mg. For exact water-temperature and steep-time targets by tea type, see our green tea steeping time guide.

Green tea vs. coffee, matcha, and black tea

Use the calculator above to compare any drink by the cup or across a full day, or check the static reference table below — the same figures the calculator uses:

DrinkServingTypical caffeineRange
Green tea (steeped)8 oz~35 mg25–45 mg
White tea (steeped)8 oz~25 mg15–30 mg
Oolong (steeped)8 oz~40 mg30–50 mg
Black tea (steeped)8 oz~50 mg40–70 mg
Matcha1 tsp (2 g) whisked in 2–3 oz~65–70 mg60–80 mg
Espresso1 oz shot~63 mg60–80 mg
Brewed coffee8 oz~95 mg80–100 mg
Rooibos / herbal8 oz0 mgcaffeine-free

Three things stand out. First, green tea, white tea, and oolong sit close together — all are lightly oxidized (or not at all) and brewed at similar, sub-boiling temperatures, so their caffeine ranges overlap. Second, matcha is the outlier among true teas: because you consume the whole ground leaf instead of steeping and discarding it, a standard serving carries close to double steeped green tea's caffeine. Third, an espresso shot and a cup of green tea land in surprisingly different places despite both being small, concentrated pours — espresso's shorter, high-pressure extraction pulls a lot more caffeine out of a lot less liquid.

Worth noting: white tea, which many people assume is the lowest-caffeine "real" tea, actually overlaps with green tea's range rather than sitting reliably below it — the buds and young leaves used for white tea can carry a comparable amount of caffeine to sencha, even though white tea is processed less than green tea.

Why green tea caffeine numbers vary online

Search around and you'll find green tea caffeine figures ranging from under 10 mg to well over 60 mg for what's described as a single cup. The gap usually comes down to what's being measured, not a real disagreement about the tea. Some sources report caffeine for a small 6 oz cup; others for a full 8 oz mug. Some quote a light, quick-steeped cup; others quote a strong, long-steeped one. Agricultural products like tea also naturally produce a range rather than one fixed number, since caffeine content shifts with growing conditions, harvest timing, and how the leaf is processed.

This page standardizes on one convention throughout: caffeine per 8 oz cup of steeped green tea, cross-checked against the USDA and published tea-caffeine sources cited below. The comparator tool above and every table on this page pull from that same dataset, so the numbers won't drift depending on which section you're reading.

Decaf and low-caffeine green tea options

If you want the flavor without the caffeine, two routes get you there. Decaffeinated green tea goes through a process that removes most — not all — of its caffeine, so a decaf cup still carries a small residual amount rather than being truly caffeine-free. Rooibos and herbal tisanes aren't tea at all; they don't come from the Camellia sinensis plant, so they contain 0 mg of caffeine with nothing to remove.

Shorter steep times and cooler water also lower caffeine somewhat without switching teas, though the effect is modest — brewing technique shifts you within green tea's 25–45 mg range, not out of it entirely. If you're trying to cut caffeine meaningfully rather than marginally, switching to a decaf green tea or a caffeine-free tisane does more than adjusting steep time on regular green tea.

Green tea, caffeine, and L-theanine

Green tea pairs its caffeine with L-theanine, an amino acid found almost exclusively in tea leaves. Published research has looked at how the two compounds interact together: Kelly and colleagues (2008, Journal of Nutrition) reported that L-theanine combined with caffeine was associated with changes in alpha-band brain activity and attention-task performance compared with either compound alone. That describes what the study measured — it isn't a promise about how any individual cup will make you feel, and responses to caffeine and L-theanine vary by person, tolerance, and how much you drink.

Matcha delivers a higher dose of both caffeine and L-theanine than steeped green tea per serving, since the whole leaf is consumed rather than steeped and discarded — see our full matcha vs green tea comparison for the numbers, or our dedicated L-theanine and caffeine in tea page for the research in more depth.

Is green tea's caffeine a lot?

At roughly 35 mg per 8 oz cup, a single serving of green tea is a modest share of the general daily reference published for healthy adults — the U.S. FDA has cited about 400 mg per day as a level not generally associated with dangerous, negative effects for most healthy adults. That reference covers total caffeine intake across everything you drink in a day, not any single cup, so it's worth counting coffee, tea, and other caffeinated drinks together rather than green tea in isolation. At the ~35 mg typical figure, it would take roughly eleven 8 oz cups to reach that reference point — far more than most people drink in a day, and more a reflection of how mild green tea's caffeine is per serving than a target to aim for. People who are pregnant, caffeine-sensitive, or managing a health condition should talk to a healthcare provider about what caffeine level is appropriate for them.

For a full side-by-side on flavor, prep, and nutrients beyond caffeine, see matcha vs green tea. To see how green tea compares against black tea more broadly, see green tea vs black tea.

This describes published research and general information, not medical or dietary advice.

faqs.q: Does green tea have more or less caffeine than coffee?
faqs.a: Less. An 8 oz cup of steeped green tea has about 25–45 mg of caffeine (typically ~35 mg), while an 8 oz brewed coffee has about 95 mg — roughly three times as much.

faqs.q: Does steeping green tea longer increase its caffeine?
faqs.a: Yes. Caffeine extracts quickly, so a longer steep and hotter water both pull out more of it — that's part of why green tea's typical range spans 25–45 mg rather than one fixed number. See our steeping-time guide for exact time and temperature targets.

faqs.q: Is it okay to drink green tea before bed?
faqs.a: Green tea's ~35 mg per cup is roughly a third of a coffee's caffeine, but caffeine sensitivity varies by person, and even a modest amount can affect sleep for some people close to bedtime. If caffeine affects your sleep, drinking green tea earlier in the day or choosing a caffeine-free tisane is worth considering.

faqs.q: Does green tea or black tea have more caffeine?
faqs.a: Black tea is higher — about 50 mg per 8 oz cup (range 40–70 mg) — compared with green tea's typical ~35 mg (range 25–45 mg). Both come from the same plant; the difference in typical caffeine comes down to how each is processed and brewed.

faqs.q: Is there a caffeine-free version of green tea?
faqs.a: Decaffeinated green tea has most of its caffeine removed but retains a small amount, so it isn't fully caffeine-free. Rooibos and herbal tisanes aren't made from the tea plant at all, so they contain 0 mg of caffeine naturally.
